newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street seen opening lower amid profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street seen opening lower amid profit-taking.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to extend losses at the open on Friday, as investors continue to take profits off the table after a rise in bond yields sent share prices tumbling yesterday.

"It looks as if the market will follow yesterday's performance, which was sloppy and on the down side," Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co said. "We could see continued profit-taking. For a long time, this market has ignored the negatives and accentuated the positives."

On Thursday, the Dow industrials slid 71 points to finish at 8188, posting losses as bond prices fell. Analysts said a rise in the long bond yield to above 6.50 percent gave investors an excuse to sell.
A mixed reaction to the U.S. Treasury auction of $10 billion in 30-year bonds and increased inflation concerns triggered weakness in the bond market, they said.
Blue chip stocks, many of which are trading at high valuations, had depended on lower bond yields to rise. If bonds were sluggish, analysts said stocks could open lower.

"We'll probably get a lower open," Hildegard Zagorski, an analyst at Prudential Securities, said. "The bond market went down yesterday, then the stock market went down. Plus, it's a Friday in the summer. It's not anything serious, but the stock market has been long overdue for some sort of shakeout."
In early trade, the Standard & Poor's 500 futures index lost 3.30 points to 952.90.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury slipped 6/32 to yield 6.54 percent.
There was no economic activity due on Friday to guide market direction.
Next week, stocks and bonds would turn to the producer and consumer price index data to gauge inflation, as well as the national report on retail sales.
On Friday, the technology sector would also digest earnings from America Online Inc, which posted a fourth quarter loss of $0.12 per share, including what it called timing adjustments.

Before these adjustments, the Internet online service company reported a profit of $0.09 per share compared with $0.14 per share in last year's fourth quarter and a First Call consensus estimate of $0.07 per share.
In other markets, the dollar was trading at 118.42/52 yen in Tokyo. In Europe, the dollar edged towards session lows against the mark, trading at 1.8599/06 marks.
Japan's Nikkei average closed up 128.61 points, or 0.66 percent, at 19,604.46.
In London, the FTSE 100 was off 49.4 at 5037.4.
U.S. stocks were mixed in quiet London trading. Shares of Boeing Co firmed amid growing hopes the aerospace company would win a $3 billion contract with India.
The Wall Street Journal said in its Heard on the Street column that speculation has increased about the possibility of Chase Manhattan Corp buying a securities firm.
The New York Times said in its Market Place column that mutual funds have already made 1997 the second-best year ever for stock funds, and bond funds are doing well too.
